findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TMQ1 Monitoring Report 26_27
findings.headline: Non-treasury investments of £61.3m showing net income outflows of £2,869k
findings.detail: The council holds £61.3m in non-treasury investments: £27.0m investment property (offices, commercial units, Otterpool property), £8.6m Oportunitas subsidiary, and £25.7m Otterpool Park LLP (£23.8m loan, £1.9m equity). findings.matters: Non-treasury investments represent concentrated higher-risk exposure in development projects and property; negative net income flows suggest project delays, costs, or valuation challenges; Otterpool Park (£25.7m, 44% of non-treasury portfolio) is a major single project exposure requiring lender scrutiny.

findings.quote: The net income and rate of return excludes the impact of any unrealised property valuation gains or losses. findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TMQ1 Monitoring Report 26_27
findings.headline: Borrowing costs £5,092k projected on budget despite PWLB rates 5.04-6.50% during quarter

findings.matters: Interest cost control is a primary pressure for all councils, and accurate budget tracking in high rates demonstrates competent treasury management supported by diversified investment income.
findings.figures: Borrowing cost £5,092k with zero variance; General Fund cost £3,185k; investment income £881k; net cost £2,304k; PWLB 5-year rates 5.04-5.49%, 20-year 6.02-6.50%
findings.quote: The total cost of borrowing is projected to be £5,092k, mainly due to additional borrowing for the HRA to support the purchase of temporary accommodation, and long-term rates remaining high.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TMQ1 Monitoring Report 26_27
findings.headline: HRA borrowing of £56.6m with 0.4% PWLB rate discount available until March 2027
findings.detail: The council holds £56.6m Housing Revenue Account borrowing at an average rate of 3.94%, representing 50% of total debt. The Public Works Loan Board offers HRA-specific loans at a rate 0.4% below the standard certainty rate until 31 March 2027. This creates a refinancing window for £4m of HRA loans maturing during the period and potentially up to £10m of new HRA borrowing to support temporary accommodation purchases.
findings.matters: HRA debt management and affordability is a core lender concern; rate discounts are time-limited so finance directors track refinancing opportunities; new temporary accommodation borrowing impacts HRA financial sustainability.

This discounted rate is to support local authorities borrowing for the Housing Revenue Account and for refinancing existing HRA loans, providing a window of opportunity for HRA-related borrowing and to replace the Council's £4m loans relating to the HRA maturing during this time frame and potential new HRA borrowing of up to £10m.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - Oportunitas Outturn and Q1
findings.headline: Council financed £6.9m of Oportunitas investment through prudential borrowing
findings.detail: Since 2014, Folkestone and Hythe council has invested approximately £11.7m in its property company, with £6.9m funded through prudential borrowing and £4.8m from Council reserves. The council's General Fund meets the annual capital financing costs of the borrowed amount.
findings.matters: A significant use of council borrowing capacity; the company's financial performance directly impacts the council's budget through debt servicing costs and expected returns on the investment.
findings.figures: £11.7m total investment; £6.9m prudential borrowing; £4.8m reserves
findings.quote: Since the Council established the company in 2014, it has invested approximately £11.7m to enable the company to acquire property, almost exclusively for residential lettings. £6.9m of this investment has been met by the Council using prudential borrowing, with the General Fund having to meet the annual capital financing cost arising from this.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TM Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Strategic pooled fund investments of £14m returned 6.32% total return with 4.81% income component, supporting both revenue and capital preservation targets
findings.detail: The council's externally managed multi-asset and property pooled funds (CCLA Local Authority Property Fund, CCLA Diversified Income Fund, Aegon Diversified Monthly Income Fund, Ninety-One Diversified Income Fund) generated £0.84m total return, comprising £0.64m income return used to support services in year and £0.20m unrealised capital growth. These funds represent the authority's minimum forecast liquid reserves over the medium term and are structured to deliver returns in excess of inflation.
findings.matters: Shows how core reserves can be deployed to generate returns above cash rates; peer councils and lenders assess whether minimum liquidity reserve strategy is self-funding
findings.figures: Pooled funds total value £13.5m; total return £0.84m (6.32%); income return £0.64m (4.81%); capital growth £0.20m (1.50%)
findings.quote: The funds generated a total increase in value of £0.84m or 6.32% compared to their value at 31 March 2025, comprising an income return of £0.64m (4.81%) which is used to support services in year, and £0.20m (1.50%) of unrealised capital growth.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TM Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Net treasury interest cost came in £1.090m below budget at £3.350m, with investment income outperforming forecast and short-term borrowing costs managing better than expected
findings.detail: Interest received from treasury investments totalled £1.212m against estimate of £1.085m (£126k better), while actual borrowing remained lower than budget with short-term rates remaining higher than anticipated. For the General Fund specifically, impact was £102k against estimate of £2.146m, with the difference due to £1.477m of capitalized interest on Otterpool Park development (against £0 budgeted).
findings.matters: Shows effective treasury management delivering better cash income than forecast and better control of borrowing costs; important for assessing financial resilience
findings.figures: Net Interest Cost £3.350m actual versus £4.440m estimate (variance £1.090m favourable); interest received £1.212m versus £1.085m estimate
findings.quote: The decrease in the net borrowing cost to the General Fund of £1,090k is mainly due to; - i) Higher than anticipated investment income received £126k from its strategic pooled fund investments and money market deposits, and ii) interest on short term borrowing remained higher than anticipated and less actual borrowing compared to budget.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TM Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increased £15.8m to £172.6m, with growth in capital spending on Otterpool Park development, HRA housing, and Changing Tides funded by £10.3m new external borrowing and £5.5m increased internal borrowing
findings.detail: Capital expenditure included Otterpool Park Garden Town development (£4.1m), HRA projects (£9.3m), Changing Tides (£0.8m) and waste vehicle purchase (£0.1m). Rather than borrowing the full amount externally, the council increased internal borrowing (using cash reserves and balances) to £54.8m, covering 32% of the CFR. This reflects the council's strategy to reduce risk and keep interest costs low by maintaining borrowing and investments below their underlying levels.
findings.matters: Lenders and peer councils need to understand the debt trajectory and how the council is funding its capital programme; growing CFR with controlled external borrowing suggests sustainable funding strategy
findings.figures: CFR £172.6m (up from £156.8m); external borrowing £117.8m (up £10.3m); internal borrowing £54.8m (up £5.5m)
findings.quote: The increase in the Council's CFR to £172.6m is due to capital expenditure in 2025/26 including the Otterpool Park Garden Town development (£4.1m), HRA projects (£9.3m), Changing Tides (£0.8m) and Purchase of Waste Vehicle (£0.1m)

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report - TM Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council breached maturity structure indicator with 43% of borrowing due within 12 months against 30% target at March 2026, but has since returned to compliance
findings.detail: The breach occurred because Arlingclose advised in March 2026 to pause long-term PWLB borrowing following significant increases in gilt yields driven by macroeconomic volatility and the US/Israel-Iran conflict. Complying with the indicator would have required fixing long-term rates at a substantial premium; instead the council used short-term borrowing. The council has since returned to compliance during summer 2026 as market conditions improved.
findings.matters: Maturity structure management is fundamental to managing refinancing and interest rate risk; lenders assess whether breach reflects risk acceptance or temporary market positioning
findings.figures: 43% of £117.8m total borrowing (£50.6m) due within 12 months; £41.2m short-term borrowing against £76.6m long-term
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, 43% of the Council's borrowing was due to mature within twelve months.

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Council breached borrowing maturity indicator with 43% of debt due within 12 months versus 30% target, but has returned to compliance
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, the council held 43% of borrowing due to mature within 12 months, exceeding the 30% prudential indicator maximum. The council deliberately paused longer-term PWLB borrowing in March 2026 following treasury advisor Arlingclose guidance during elevated market volatility caused by the US/Israel war with Iran; 10-year PWLB rates had risen to 5.88% (from 5.13% at period start). The council instead used short-term local authority loans at 4.0-7.0%, accepting near-term refinancing risk to avoid locking in elevated long-term rates. Compliance has been restored by summer 2026 as market conditions improved.
findings.matters: High proportion of debt maturing within short periods creates refinancing risk and exposure to rate movements if loans must be rolled over; however this breach was a deliberate tactical choice during volatile markets and has been actively managed.
findings.figures: 43% of borrowing due within 12 months vs 30% target; PWLB 10-year rates 5.13% to 5.88%; Short-term LA loan rates 4.0-4.5% most of year, rising to 5.0-7.0% at year-end
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026, 43% of the Council's borrowing was due to mature within twelve months.

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Non-treasury investment portfolio of £61.3m is generating -£2.6m negative cash income despite showing 7.68% book value returns
findings.detail: The council holds £61.3m in non-treasury investments including investment property (£27.0m) and subsidiary loans and equity (£34.4m). Net income is forecast at -£2,639k for 2026/27. Book value returns appear positive at 7.68% because they include unrealised property valuations; however the council discloses that net income figures exclude these unrealised gains. Negative cash is driven by development project loans (Otterpool Park LLP -£1,834k, Oportunitas -£310k) and property portfolio losses (-£495k), indicating the portfolio is in growth phase and not self-funding.
findings.matters: A £61m portfolio that is currently consuming cash (negative £2.6m annually) and relies on unrealised valuations for positive returns represents concentration risk; if property valuations fall or projects encounter delays, the portfolio could move to loss positions and further deplete reserves.
findings.figures: Total non-treasury investments £61.3m; Forecasted net income 2026/27 -£2,639k; Book value return 7.68%; Otterpool Park LLP -£1,834k; Oportunitas -£310k; Property -£495k
findings.quote: The net income and rate of return excludes the impact of any unrealised property valuation gains or losses.

findings.matters: A £23.8m loan to a single development project that is currently negative cash-generative represents material development and counterparty risk; lenders need clarity on project viability and when the council will receive cash returns.
findings.figures: Otterpool Park LLP loan £21.3m → £23.8m (+£2.5m); Total exposure £25.7m (loan £23.8m + equity £1.9m); Forecasted 2026/27 net income -£1,834k
findings.quote: The increase in the Council's CFR to £172.6m is due to capital expenditure in 2025/26 including the Otterpool Park Garden Town development (£4.1m)

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Treasury Management Annual Report 25-26
findings.headline: Capital financing requirement and borrowing increased 10% due to capital programme expansion, particularly Otterpool Park Garden Town
findings.detail: The council's capital financing requirement increased from £156.8m to £172.6m (+£15.8m or 10%) during 2025/26, driven by capital expenditure funded through prudential borrowing. findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 – Borrowing, loans held at 31 March 2026
findings.headline: £41 million of borrowing from other councils matures between June and October 2026.
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2026, the council held £41 million borrowed from nine other councils: Portsmouth (£5m, due 13 Aug 2026), Milton Keynes (£5m, due 22 Jun 2026), East Sussex (£5m, due 14 Jul 2026), Northern Ireland Housing Executive (£5m, due 8 Oct 2026), Cornwall (£5m, due 13 Oct 2026), Brentwood (£5m, due 17 Aug 2026), Stevenage (£3m, due 3 Aug 2026), Preston (£4m, due 22 Jun 2026), and Staffordshire (£4m, due 15 Jun 2026). All are fixed-rate loans maturing within 3–6 months of the report date.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial position would need to understand whether the council can refinance this material portion of its borrowing portfolio (35 per cent of total borrowing of £117.8m) within the next three to six months.
findings.figures: £41 million; maturities June–October 2026; interest rates 4.22–5.6%; total borrowing £117,842,038.80

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Updated General Fund Medium Term Capital Programme 26_27
findings.headline: Borrowing requirement increases by £520k to £60.2m to fund capital programme overspend
findings.detail: Capital borrowing has risen from the previously approved £59.68m to £60.2m, a £520k increase required to cover capital programme overruns and funding shortfalls. The borrowing profile is front-loaded (£14.6m in 26/27) with the majority concentrated in 2030/31 (£34.1m) for Otterpool Park delivery.
findings.matters: Additional borrowing to cover programme overruns increases debt service costs and leverage ratios. A £60m+ borrowing programme with heavy concentration in a single future year creates refinancing and rate risk.
findings.figures: Borrowing approved £59,680k, now projected £60,200k; increase variance £520k

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Updated General Fund Medium Term Capital Programme 26_27
findings.headline: Council drawing on reserves to fund £706k of new capital projects added in 26/27
findings.detail: Four new capital projects totalling over £700k are being funded directly from reserves in 2026/27: Digital Lifeline Equipment (£256k from Financial Resilience reserve, Cabinet approval 24.06.26), Mermaid Beach Storm Damage Repairs (£200k from carry-forward reserve, Council approval 22.07.26), Martello Lakes Sports Facilities (£250k from Leisure and General Fund reserves, Council approval 22.07.26), and Ship Street Site (£102k from capital receipts). Each project had zero prior budget allocation.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund new capital reduces financial resilience and the council's capacity to absorb unforeseen costs or revenue pressures. Drawing down reserves to add projects mid-year signals either inadequate initial planning or emerging new pressures.
findings.figures: Digital Lifeline Equipment 256; Mermaid Beach 200; Martello Lakes 250; Ship Street 132
findings.quote: New Project for 26/27 funded from £180k Leisure reserve and £70k GF reserve - approved by Council 22.07.26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Updated General Fund Medium Term Capital Programme 26_27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park Garden Town £34.1m (71% of total) committed to 2030/31 final year
findings.detail: Otterpool Park Delivery is heavily back-loaded, with £34.1m of the total £47.6m scheme cost concentrated in the final year of the MTCP (2030/31). Spend in the four prior years (26/27-29/30) averages only £3.4m per annum. This creates acute delivery and financing risk in a single year.
findings.matters: Concentration of 71% of a £47.6m scheme into the final year creates both delivery risk (can the scheme physically be built?) and financing risk (can borrowing of £34m+ be arranged for one year at acceptable cost?). This is material to debt sustainability forecasts beyond the current MTCP.
findings.figures: Otterpool Park total £47,606k; 2030/31 projection £34,096k; prior four years total £13.5m

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Draft Treasury Management 2026-27 - Quarter 1
findings.headline: Treasury risk controls exceed all targets: portfolio credit rating A+ (vs A target), liquid reserves £11.7m (vs £5m target), interest rate exposure minimized.
findings.detail: Council reports full CIPFA Code compliance with all key risk indicators exceeding targets. Portfolio credit rating A+ versus A target, reflecting conservative counterparty management. Liquid cash within three months £11.7m versus £5m minimum target, providing substantial buffer against market stress or cash flow shocks. Interest rate exposure £113k versus £280k annual limit, indicating minimal rate vulnerability.
findings.matters: Compliance with all risk limits and exceeding of target buffers demonstrates robust treasury governance and provides resilience against market volatility or refinancing shocks.
findings.figures: Credit rating A+ (target A). Liquid cash £11.7m within 3 months (target £5m). Interest rate exposure £113k (limit £280k).

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Draft Treasury Management 2026-27 - Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council maintaining stable borrowing costs despite long-term rates remaining elevated, through internal borrowing from cash reserves.
findings.detail: Total borrowing cost projected at £5,092k, unchanged from original estimate, despite Treasury's acknowledgment that long-term rates remain high. Stability achieved through internal borrowing strategy using available cash reserves (£54.8m) to minimize reliance on new external borrowing at elevated rates. This provides buffer against rate fluctuations, though it is cyclical; additional short-term borrowing is anticipated in latter financial year months as cash inflows decline.
findings.matters: Effective cost management in a rising-rate environment demonstrates strong treasury management, but dependence on cyclical cash inflows creates vulnerability if rate environment deteriorates further.
findings.figures: Total borrowing cost £5,092k (on budget, no variance). Internal borrowing £54.8m available. 5-year PWLB rates 5.07%, 20-year 6.50%.
findings.quote: The total cost of borrowing is projected to be £5,092k, mainly due to additional borrowing for the HRA to support the purchase of temporary accommodation, and long-term rates remaining high

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Draft Treasury Management 2026-27 - Quarter 1
findings.headline: Commercial property investment portfolio returning only 1.89%, significantly below borrowing costs (4.18%) and treasury investment returns (4.53%).
findings.detail: The council holds £27m in investment property generating £509k net income (1.89% return). Major portfolio components underperform: Otterpool property £8.5m at 0.88%, offices £16.2m at 1.80%. Only commercial units (£2.2m) achieve acceptable 6.40% return. Returns reflect weak commercial property market conditions, with capital returns described as "broadly flat to modestly negative" and elevated financing costs limiting income growth.
findings.matters: The council's £27m property portfolio is generating returns below its borrowing costs, indicating suboptimal capital allocation and concentration risk in a cyclically weak asset class with uncertain recovery prospects.
findings.figures: £27m investment property portfolio, £509k net income, 1.89% blended return. Otterpool 0.88%, offices 1.80%, commercial units 6.40%. Borrowing cost 4.18%, treasury investments 4.53%.
findings.quote: UK commercial property capital returns were broadly flat to modestly negative over the quarter, with performance continuing to be driven primarily by income rather than capital growth

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Compliance with specific investment and borrowing limits and
findings.headline: Council held 43% of borrowing at under 12 months maturity, exceeding 30% approved limit
findings.detail: During 2025/26, the council deliberately kept a higher proportion of its debt portfolio at short maturities, reaching 43% against an approved upper limit of 30%. This was a deliberate strategy to avoid locking in elevated interest rates during volatile market conditions.
findings.matters: A lender cares about refinancing risk; the council faces significant debt repayment obligations in the next 12 months and has accepted this concentration of short-term maturity risk to manage interest rate risk
findings.figures: 43% actual vs 30% upper limit
findings.quote: Interest rates remained elevated throughout 2025/26 with heightened market volatility caused by macroeconomic events and therefore a higher percentage of the debt portfolio was kept at very short maturity dates of less than twelve months rather than taking out debt in the medium-term period of one to five years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 – Compliance with specific investment and borrowing limits and
findings.headline: Council breached approved interest rate exposure limit due to expanded capital programme
findings.detail: The council's actual interest rate exposure (£281,000 impact from a 1% rise) exceeded the approved limit of £220,000. The council explains that the original approved limits did not account for the maximum new or replacement borrowing the council could be liable for under the latest capital programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council has departed from approved treasury management limits and has taken on greater interest rate risk than originally planned
findings.figures: Actual £281,000 vs approved limit £220,000
findings.quote: The actual upper limit on the one-year revenue impact of a 1% rise and fall in rates exceeds the limits set for the year. The original approved limits did not fully reflect the maximum amount of new or replacement borrowing the Council could be liable to take up over the next 12 months.

findings.paper_title: HRA Cabinet Report - Revenue and Capital BM Qtr 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Council flags medium risk of deferring HRA capital expenditure into 2027/28 due to delivery capacity constraints
findings.detail: The council identifies insufficient capacity as a medium likelihood, medium seriousness risk to the HRA capital programme. This suggests parts of the £32.08m capital programme may not be delivered in-year.
findings.matters: A £32m capital programme is material for housing delivery. If the council cannot deliver it in the planned year due to capacity constraints, this affects housing supply timelines, contractor scheduling, and the financing assumptions built into the budget.

findings.paper_title: FPSC Report - Budget Strategy 2027-28
findings.headline: General Fund reserves of £22.71m are available but the council explicitly acknowledges using them to bridge budget gaps only works on a one-off annual basis
findings.detail: Total General Fund reserves at 1 April 2026 were £22.71m (including £4.66m in general reserve). The council's strategy includes using reserves to cover annual budget gaps, but it acknowledges this approach 'only reduces the shortfall for the year it is applied' and that permanent reduction in the financial gap requires permanent changes to expenditure or revenue.
findings.matters: While reserves provide a buffer, they are finite; sustained use to cover structural deficits indicates the council is not addressing the underlying spending/revenue imbalance and would leave it vulnerable to depletion

findings.headline: Prices Parade Planning Project written off for £3.4m, though offset by use of Financial Resilience reserve
findings.detail: A capital project (Prices Parade Planning) was written off entirely this year with a loss of £3.4m. The council covered this from the Financial Resilience reserve, meaning it did not hit the outturn, but the reserve had to absorb a major capital failure.
findings.matters: Capital project failures are routine; having a reserve to absorb them is prudent. But a £3.4m write-off on a single project signals either poor planning, scheme failure, or overly optimistic initial estimates. It also depletes the reserve meant to cushion other shocks.
findings.figures: £3.4m written off
findings.quote: Corporate Estates & Development - £3.081m - unfavourable variance is driven mainly by the Prices Parade Planning Project being written off this year (£3.4m). This is offset by a planned transfer from the Financial Resilience reserve.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: £5.5m in unspent budget being carried forward to next year specifically to address forecast funding gaps
findings.detail: The council is holding £5.468m as carry forwards, described explicitly as needed to 'address forecast funding gaps' in 2026/27. This is a large proportion of annual movements and signals the council knows the coming year will have a structural funding shortfall it is pre-funding with this year's underspends and carried budget.
findings.matters: Forward carry forwards labelled against 'funding gaps' is a council's way of saying 'we do not have enough money next year and we are trying to avoid a deficit by holding this back.' It suggests deteriorating financial position and medium-term sustainability concerns.
findings.quote: provisional operational carry forwards of £5.468m have been approved by the Section 151 Officer and CLT as budgeted revenue expenditure relating to 2025/26 that will be carried forward to 2026/27 to reinvest in frontline services and address forecast funding gaps.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Service budgets overran by £3m, worsened by £650k since Q3, driven chiefly by temporary accommodation pressures
findings.detail: Service spend came in £3.034m worse than approved budget—not a small variance but a deterioration. It got £654k worse between Q3 and outturn. The primary driver is temporary accommodation, which appears across multiple service lines (Governance & Finance, Homelessness & Housing Options). The council's underlying service spending is not under control.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget shortfalls are one-off or structural. A deteriorating position between Q3 and outturn, driven by recurring demand (homelessness), signals the council cannot forecast or control costs in its core services.
findings.figures: £3.034m unfavourable variance on services; £654k deterioration from Q3
findings.quote: The overall spend against service budgets for the year has resulted in an unfavourable position of £3.034m (Appendix A, 'Total for Service'), a movement of £654k to Q3 projections, driven in large part by temporary accommodation pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025.26 General Fund Revenue Provisional Outturn Report
findings.headline: Funding loss of £2.4m from Kent County Council discontinuing a support scheme, forcing the council to fund temporary accommodation costs from reserves
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £2.404m of income from rent rebates, housing benefits for temporary accommodation, council tax benefits and council tax reduction scheme, funded via Kent County Council. KCC discontinued the scheme mid-year. The council is now covering this gap using the Homelessness Prevention Grant reserve, revealing a significant and growing homelessness burden.
findings.matters: Loss of external funding combined with rising temporary accommodation need means the council is depleting reserves to meet a current demand that has no sustainable funding answer. This is a structural problem, not a one-off.
findings.quote: £2.404m of expenditure for rent rebates, housing benefits [temporary accommodation], council tax benefits and council tax reduction scheme budgeted income that is no longer being received; this is based on a Kent County Council decision to discontinue the scheme.

findings.paper_title: Folkestone Hythe District Council_Letter on 2025-26 Audit Timelines
findings.headline: New financial system implementation during 2026-27 audit and reporting period
findings.detail: The council is implementing a new financial system in 2026-27, coinciding with the period when audit deadlines are at their tightest. The auditors note they will coordinate to ensure the audit process works alongside the system implementation.
findings.matters: Financial system implementations carry inherent risks around data migration and control gaps that could affect the council's ability to close accounts and meet audit deadlines during a critical compliance period.
findings.figures: System implementation 2026-27; audit deadline 30 November 2026 (Grant Thornton target); statutory deadline 30 November 2027
findings.quote: We recognise that you will be implementing a new financial system in 2026/27 and we will work with you to ensure that the audit process works in tandem with this process.

findings.paper_title: Folkestone Hythe District Council_Letter on 2025-26 Audit Timelines
findings.headline: MHCLG assessing council's ability to maintain and rebuild assurance by 31 July 2026
findings.detail: Grant Thornton reports that MHCLG has requested a case-by-case assessment of whether Folkestone and Hythe can maintain and, where necessary, rebuild assurance. This assessment is due 31 July 2026 and is described as key to demonstrating the council's capability to meet the new audit deadlines.
findings.matters: The language 'rebuild assurance' signals MHCLG may have identified governance or audit concerns, and wants auditor confirmation the council can recover and meet tightened statutory deadlines.
findings.figures: Assessment due 31 July 2026
findings.quote: MHCLG have asked us as a firm to report by 31 July 2026, on a case-by-case basis, our assessment of the Council's ability to both maintain and where necessary rebuild assurance

findings.paper_title: Folkestone and Hythe DC Audit Findings Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £3.57m valuation error discovered and corrected in Oportunitas Ltd equity investment
findings.detail: The Council's wholly-owned subsidiary Oportunitas Ltd (providing affordable housing) was valued at £734k at March 2024. During 2025 valuation work, material errors were identified: the discount rate was incorrectly applied and applied to interim cash flows rather than full-year figures. The revised valuation is £4.3m, a £3.57m understatement. Corrected via prior period adjustment in 2025 accounts.
findings.matters: A five-fold valuation error indicates material weaknesses in the Council's asset valuation processes, particularly for complex unlisted investments. This raises questions about reliability of valuations across the asset base (£289.54m in land and buildings, council dwellings and investment properties).
findings.figures: Prior value £734k, corrected value £4.3m, error of £3.57m (material misstatement)
findings.quote: Correcting these inputs resulted in a revised fair value of £4.3m, meaning the investment was understated by £3.57m in the 2024 financial statements. This misstatement is material and qualifies as a prior period error.

findings.paper_title: Folkestone and Hythe DC Audit Findings Report 24-25 Final
findings.headline: £3.4m from Princes Parade development will be written off to revenue in 2025/26
findings.detail: The Council capitalised £3.4m of costs for a Princes Parade development (housing and leisure centre) from April 2022. The project was paused in 2022/23 due to difficult economic conditions and formally ended following a public consultation in June 2025. The £3.4m remains on the balance sheet as assets under construction and the Council intends to write the entire amount to revenue in 2025/26, creating a material one-time charge.
findings.matters: A significant capital scheme has been wound down with full write-off to follow, indicating capital scheme management issues and creating material budget impact in the next financial year.
findings.figures: £3.4m capitalised costs brought forward from April 2023; represents 130% of materiality (£2.6m)
findings.quote: The development was initially capitalised as an asset under construction (AUC), with costs of £3.4m brought forward as at 1 April 2022/23 with management intending to write off this balance within the 2025/26 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Council has identified 'a number of demand-led budgets which are difficult to control' as a strategic risk
findings.detail: As part of budget assumptions, the council explicitly notes it is responsible for multiple demand-led budget areas that are 'difficult to control.' This is flagged as part of the strategic risk assessment that informed the council's minimum reserve levels.
findings.matters: Demand-led services (typically social care, housing support) are hard to forecast and control. Unplanned spending in these areas can quickly erode reserves. The council's explicit identification of this as a control risk is material to reserve adequacy and financial resilience.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The council is responsible for a number of demand -led budgets which are difficult to control.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: General Fund minimum reserve of £1.5m is contingent on delivering savings proposals over the planning period
findings.detail: Council sets minimum General Fund reserve at £1.5m based on strategic risk assessment. The policy states this minimum 'will be monitored and should be addressed as savings proposals are developed and implemented.' This makes reserve adequacy conditional on executing the council's savings plan.
findings.matters: If the council fails to deliver planned savings, it will face pressure either to cut deeper or to breach its own minimum reserve level. This signals that current reserve levels depend on successful delivery of savings proposals and suggests underlying financial pressure.
findings.figures: General Fund minimum £1.5m
findings.quote: This level will be monitored and should be addressed as savings proposals are developed and implemented over the term of this plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation in progress; external auditors require reserves maintained prudently through transition
findings.detail: Council is undergoing LGR. Both central government and external auditors (Grant Thornton) have mandated that reserve usage cannot be changed as a result of LGR, and reserves must be maintained at prudent levels through reorganisation and by successor bodies.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change affecting the council's independence and future organisation. This constraint on reserve usage during transition is a lending risk factor and signals that both auditors and government are watching reserve discipline closely.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: The guidance from both Central Government and external parties such as our external auditors Grant Thornton have been very clear in that the planned use of reserves, similar to the disposal of assets should not be changed as a direct result of LGR.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6 - Council Reserves Policy
findings.headline: Reserves reduced to 'adequate rather than excessive' level following major capital investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool
findings.detail: Council has deliberately drawn down reserves over recent years to fund capital investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool projects and other investments, or to reduce borrowing. The council now describes reserves as 'adequate rather than excessive' - meaning the financial cushion is tight and not excessive.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's cash buffer for absorbing unexpected pressures. Reserves at 'adequate rather than excessive' level means limited room to maneuver if new risks materialise or demand-led services overspend.
findings.figures: General Fund minimum £1.5m, HRA minimum £2.0m, Capital Receipts minimum £0.5m
findings.quote: The level of reserves has, in recent years, reduced in line with planned activities such as investments in Oportunitas and Otterpool and their use for other investment or in lieu of borrowing. This strategy means that reserves are currently at an adequate rather than excessive level

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council holds £27.1m in commercial property to generate revenue offsetting declining government funding, explicitly acknowledging exposure to market demand, void tenancy, and capital value risks
findings.detail: The council has invested £27.1m in commercial property (largest: Connect 38 in Ashford at £16.4m; Otterpool Park land £8.5m) with the explicit purpose of generating capital gains and revenue streams to replace declining government grants. The council acknowledges principal risks include 'fluctuations in future demand of the market including competition, risk of void tenancies, fall in capital values etc.'
findings.matters: The council has substituted declined grant funding with higher-risk commercial property investment as a revenue source. Market downturns, property voids, or capital value falls would directly reduce revenue available for service delivery.
findings.figures: £27.1m commercial investments; £16.4m Connect 38; £8.5m Otterpool Park land; net income £1.6m (2025/26 forecast)
findings.quote: With central government financial support for local public services declining, the Authority previously invested in commercial property and land with the intention of making capital gains or generating new revenue streams to spend on lol public services. Total commercial investments are currently valued at £27.1m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs rising to 14.2% of housing revenue by 2028/29, driven by 65% growth in housing capital financing requirement
findings.detail: HRA financing costs (interest and MRP on housing debt) are projected to rise from £1.9m in 2024/25 (9.2% of HRA revenue) to £3.5m by 2028/29 (14.2% of revenue). This is driven by the HRA capital financing requirement growing from £50.4m to £83.2m, a 65% increase, as the council accelerates capital investment in housing stock.
findings.matters: An increasing proportion of housing revenue consumed by debt service reduces resources available for repairs, maintenance, and service delivery. At 14.2% of revenue, debt service represents a significant operational burden.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: £1.9m (2024/25) to £3.5m (2028/29); proportion of revenue: 9.2% to 14.2%; HRA CFR: £50.4m to £83.2m
findings.quote: HRA Financing costs (£m) 1.9 2.4 2.9 3.3 3.5 Proportion of net revenue stream 9.2% 11.4% 12.9% 13.8% 14.2%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: External grant funding for capital projects fell 41% year-on-year, forcing increased reliance on debt to finance the capital programme
findings.detail: External sources (government grants and contributions) funding capital expenditure fell from £20.3m in 2025/26 forecast to £12.0m in 2026/27 budget. To maintain the £46.4m capital programme, the council increased debt financing from £14.4m to £20.1m, a 40% increase.
findings.matters: Declining grant-in-aid increases reliance on borrowed money to fund capital, raising debt service costs in future years. It signals reduced external support and forces debt-financed capital strategies.
findings.figures: External sources 2025/26: £20.3m; 2026/27: £12.0m (41% decline). Debt financing: £14.4m to £20.1m (40% increase)
findings.quote: External sources 5.9 20.3 12.0 4.5 0.5

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development, the largest service investment, expected to generate no capital receipts over the next three years
findings.detail: Otterpool Park is the council's largest service investment (part of £34m total service investments), with £8.5m held in land and property and £4.6m capital expenditure budgeted for 2026/27. The council explicitly states no capital receipts are anticipated from the development over the three-year period to 2028/29.
findings.matters: A long-dated capital commitment with explicitly deferred or uncertain returns increases financial risk. If the development stalls, underperforms, or faces market headwinds, capital remains locked up in a non-productive asset during the forecast period.
findings.figures: £4.6m capital budget 2026/27; £8.5m land holding; £34m total service investments; £0 receipts anticipated to 2028/29
findings.quote: No capital receipts from Otterpool Park development are anticipated to be received over the three-year period to 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 Capital Strategy and MRP policy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council switching minimum revenue provision from straight-line to annuity method, backloading debt repayment to later years
findings.detail: Following a review by advisors Arlingclose in 2025/26, the council has changed its MRP calculation method from straight-line to annuity. The annuity method produces lower charges in early years and higher charges in later years over a 50-year amortisation period. This change takes effect from 2025/26.
findings.matters: A lender assessing sustainability needs to understand the debt servicing trajectory. Annuity method defers charges to later years, backloading repayment obligations when the council's revenue position may be less certain.
findings.figures: Lower early charges, higher later charges; applied to assets with useful lives up to 50 years
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council engaged its advisors to undertake a review of the MRP. As a result of the review, it was recommended to change the MRP method from straight line to annuity; this means lower charges in the early years and higher charges in later years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs are uncertain but reserved; November 2025 deadline for MHCLG submissions
findings.detail: The council notes: 'proposals for reorganisation of local government remain ongoing with the other Kent authorities ahead of the November 2025 deadline for submissions to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. A Local Government Reorganisation reserve was set up in 2025/26 to help mitigate any costs associated with reorganisation.' LGR could reshape the council's cost base and structure.
findings.matters: LGR is a material uncertainty; the reserve indicates recognition of significant one-off and potentially recurring costs ahead. Reorganisation outcomes could change the council's financial profile and risk profile.
findings.figures: LGR reserve set up in 2025/26 (amount not specified); Nov 2025 submission deadline
findings.quote: proposals for reorganisation of local government remain ongoing with the other Kent authorities ahead of the November 2025 deadline for submissions to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund reserves of £21.55m cannot bridge the structural deficit; reserves are one-time only
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'use of reserves is only a one -off (one year option) as it only reduces the shortfall for the year it is applied.' Total reserves at 1 April 2025 were £21.55m (General Reserve £5.89m). The council must solve the deficit through permanent baseline cuts or new recurring income, not reserves.
findings.matters: Finite reserves cannot bridge a multi-year structural deficit; this signals the council's reserves cannot be a crutch and that permanent solutions must be found. Reserve depletion signals financial stress.
findings.figures: Total General Fund reserves £21.55m; General Reserve £5.89m; policy minimum 10% of net cost of services
findings.quote: use of reserves is only a one -off (one year option) as it only reduces the shortfall for the year it is applied.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Pension fund triennial valuation due December 2025 with current assumption of no change—outcome uncertain
findings.detail: The council states: 'A new valuation is due in December 2025 from the pension fund actuary and will impact the 2026/27 budget. Current assumptions are no change to the pension contributions rate.' Pension valuations can significantly alter costs if funding levels or longevity assumptions move.
findings.matters: Pension contribution rate increases (often £0.5m–£2m+ for a council this size) would worsen the MTFS deficit; the assumption of no change is optimistic and a material risk.
findings.figures: Last valuation Nov 2022; new valuation due Dec 2025; current assumption zero change to contribution rate
findings.quote: A new valuation is due in December 2025 from the pension fund actuary and will impact the 2026/27 budget. Current assumptions are no change to the pension contributions rate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Pay award locks in £850k additional cost for 2026/27 on £21.6m payroll; future-year assumption of 2% may not hold
findings.detail: The council has a two-year pay settlement from April 2025. The second year (2026/27) allows £1,500 added to each salary point or 3.5%, whichever is greater, equating to 'approximately £850k.' The MTFS assumes only 2% pay growth for 2027/28 onwards, which is at risk if public-sector pay catch-up continues.
findings.matters: Pay awards are fixed costs that cannot flex when income shortfalls occur; underestimating future pay growth increases the deficit faster than currently forecast.
findings.figures: £850k cost of 2026/27 pay award on £21.6m payroll base; assumed 2% for 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: The second year of the agreement will feed into the 2026/27 budget setting process and allows for £1,500 to be added to every salary point on all salary scales or 3.5%, whichever is the greater amount. This equates to approximately £850k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation 'subsidy gap' is growing; Central Government funding does not match private-market costs
findings.detail: The council identifies this as a major ongoing pressure: 'there is an increased service demand for temporary accommodation nationwide. Where the Council utilises private lets for the purpose of temporary accommodation, central Government does not fully fund the cost of those placements creating the 'subsidy gap'.' The council is now considering capital investment in TA properties to minimize these losses.
findings.matters: TA costs are structural and volatile; the 'subsidy gap' represents a growing unbudgeted cost with no resolution until the housing crisis eases, and capital investment in TA properties represents a significant new commitment with uncertain returns.
findings.figures: No specific gap figures quantified in this document
findings.quote: there is an increased service demand for temporary accommodation nationwide. Where the Council utilises private lets for the purpose of temporary accommodation, central Government does not fully fund the cost of those placements creating the 'subsidy gap'.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Government funding settlement expected to remain 'cash flat' with no new resources for 2026/27
findings.detail: The strategy assumes 'the LGFS will be 'cash flat' for district councils again this year, with no new funding or increase in core spending power.' This continues a pattern where Revenue Support Grant has effectively ceased (none 2018/19–2023/24) and new grants rolled in during 2025/26 were offset by removal of previous grants, creating no net gain.
findings.matters: With inflation running 3.6%–3.8% and pay awards locked at 3.5% minimum, a flat cash settlement forces real-terms service cuts or revenue-raising; this is a key driver of the MTFS deficit.
findings.figures: RSG £0.263m in 2025/26; no RSG for 2018/19–2023/24; not expected in future years
findings.quote: It is assumed that the LGFS will be 'cash flat' for district councils again this year, with no new funding or increase in core spending power.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Business Rates Reset consultation could eliminate the council's £4.1m annual business rates income entirely
findings.detail: The council currently retains £4.1m from business rates (40% of £45m+ collected, after tariffs/top-ups). A Business Rates Reset consultation outcome is expected Nov 2025 or Dec 2025. The council explicitly warns: 'there remains a risk that this council may no longer retain any Business Rates in the future. This would result in a funding gap that would need to be replaced by additional income or further savings.'
findings.matters: Loss of £4.1m (≈12% of general fund income) would open a material new funding gap that could not be closed by Council Tax alone without breaching referendum limits; this is existential risk to the budget.
findings.figures: £4.1m business rates in 2025/26; council collects £45m+ gross; retains 40% net
findings.quote: there remains a risk that this council may no longer retain any Business Rates in the future. This would result in a funding gap that would need to be replaced by additional income or further savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus funding of £432k annually is assumed to end with no replacement identified
findings.detail: The council received £0.432m NHB in 2025/26 to fund revenue. The strategy states this will now end: 'It is assumed that NHB has ended and no further payments will be received based on the Fair Funding Review consultation which deemed the scheme ineffective.' This is a permanent loss of income with no mitigation plan.
findings.matters: The permanent loss of £432k recurring income (without replacement) directly increases the structural deficit and forces either service cuts or other tax/charge increases.
findings.figures: £0.432m received in 2025/26; assumption zero from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: It is assumed that NHB has ended and no further payments will be received based on the Fair Funding Review consultation which deemed the scheme ineffective.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10 - Budget Strategy
findings.headline: Four-year MTFS forecasts cumulative deficit of £5.52m, with deficits growing to £2.9m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The published MTFS projects £723k deficit in 2026/27, rising to £2.887m in 2027/28, then £1.913m in 2028/29, totalling £5.52m over the four-year period. The council acknowledges these are structural gaps requiring permanent solutions (expenditure cuts or new recurring income), not temporary fixes.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit signals the council must make substantive service changes or revenue-raising decisions; bondholders and lenders would be concerned about the council's ability to deliver balanced budgets without service deterioration.
findings.quote: the current published MTFS from February 2025 forecast a cumulative funding gap of £5.52m over the lifetime of the MTFS to 202 8/29

findings.paper_title: Appendix 13 - GF Revenue Growth items summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Committee system restructuring assumptions have not materialized, requiring budget reversal
findings.detail: Special responsibility allowances (£128,130) and employer NI (£20,200) were reduced in 2024-25 in anticipation of moving to a committee system. These budgets are now being realigned upward because the anticipated governance change has not been implemented. The council states this is 'to counteract previous budget reduction with expectation of going over to committee system'.
findings.matters: Strategic governance restructuring planned in prior years has not been executed, creating budget volatility and raising questions about council decision-making and the stability of planned savings.
findings.quote: To counteract previous budget reduction with expectation of going over to committee system. Previous year 2024/25 budget had been reduced in anticipation of the change to Committee System and removal of Cabinet allowances. This request now is to realign the budget with the anticipated full special responsibility allowance

findings.paper_title: Appendix 13 - GF Revenue Growth items summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Council requests £28,780 salary uplift to retain Levelling Up Fund Project Support Officer; role unfilled creates "risk to project delivery" and MHCLG requirements
findings.detail: The council is requesting £28,780 for a salary uplift to retain the LUF Project Support Officer (fixed-term contract extension). The justification explicitly states that if this role is not filled, it will 'create a risk to the project delivery and FHDC's ability to deliver all the key requirements needed by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG)'.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly flagged a potential non-compliance risk with central government obligations if funding for this role is not approved, creating potential accountability questions.
findings.quote: This is a critical resource to ensure project delivery. If the role is not filled this will create a risk to the project delivery and FHDC's ability to deliver all the key requirements needed by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 13 - GF Revenue Growth items summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Homelessness and private sector housing costs rising, with reliance on unconfirmed grant and reserves
findings.detail: The council is requesting £81,500 additional budget for Private Sector housing costs, describing this as driven by 'mounting pressure on the Private Sector Offer observed throughout 2025'. Funding depends on the Homelessness Prevention Grant (allocation for 2026-27 not yet confirmed) and any overspend will be met from the Homelessness Prevention reserve. A separate £208,700 growth request for homelessness prevention activities also relies on this reserve.
findings.matters: Growing service pressure is being managed through external grants and reserves rather than base budget, while the grant allocation remains uncertain. This signals either demand pressure or cost inflation the council cannot fully absorb.
findings.quote: Increase in expenditure within Private Sector Offer. This growth request is driven by increased expenditure and mounting pressure on the Private Sector Offer observed throughout 2025... While the Homelessness Prevention Grant allocation for 2026–27 has not yet been confirmed... Any overspend from this budget is funded by the Homelessness Prevention reserve

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Statement on the robustness and adequacy of reserves
findings.headline: Council acknowledges unresolved medium-term financial strategy gap requiring further decisions over coming year
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states the council 'will need to take further decisions over the next financial year to ensure a sustainable financial position is achievable over the medium term'. The MTFS contains 'key financial issues (cumulative gap) which will need to be tackled', and there is 'significant uncertainty towards the later years of the MTFS', particularly due to uncertainty around Local Government Reform restructuring.
findings.matters: Indicates structural budget challenge beyond 2026/27; timing and magnitude of required savings remain unquantified, creating uncertainty for planning and creditworthiness
findings.figures: Gap size not quantified in this appendix
findings.quote: The Council will need to take further decisions over the next financial year to ensure a sustainable financial position is achievable over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Statement on the robustness and adequacy of reserves
findings.headline: Business rates baseline cut by £0.7m (17.5%) in government reset, representing permanent structural loss of funding
findings.detail: The government's business rates reset reduced the council's baseline from £4.0m to £3.3m. This baseline sets the foundation for all future business rates growth calculations, so the reduction is structural, not cyclical. Partially offset by increased Revenue Support Grant but the net impact is loss of a volatile, discretionary revenue source.
findings.matters: Permanent loss of a major revenue source requires either service cuts, ongoing tax rises, or reserve use; the reset also increases reliance on the more uncertain RSG stream
findings.figures: Business rates baseline cut from £4.0m to £3.3m
findings.quote: This Council saw the business rates baseline cut from just over £4.0m to £3.3m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Statement on the robustness and adequacy of reserves
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to decline by £7.1m in one year, continuing a three-year drawdown pattern
findings.detail: Combined general and earmarked reserves falling from £22.078m (1 April 2025) to £14.97m (31 March 2026). The S151 Officer explicitly acknowledges the council 'has drawn on them in the last three years' and emphasizes 'reserves can only be applied once', signalling concern about the sustainability of continued drawdown.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves limit the council's financial flexibility to absorb unexpected costs, fund strategic priorities, or manage income volatility without further drawdowns or service cuts
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £15.659m to £9.85m (down £5.8m); General reserves: £6.419m to £5.12m (down £1.3m); combined reduction of £7.1m in one year
findings.quote: Caution does need to be noted however, reserves can only be applied once and whilst the Council has a prudent record of building reserves over a number of financial years, it has drawn on them in the last three years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Contractual non-service inflation of £2.88m appears in 2029/30 with no identified offsetting savings or income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: Government non-service grants drop 72% from £4.17m to £1.16m, and Revenue Support Grant declines from £5.98m to £3.86m by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS)
findings.headline: A cumulative funding gap of £5.4m accumulates by 2029/30, with no identified funding source in this forecast.
findings.detail: The council forecasts balanced budgets in 2025/26 and 2026/27, but deficits emerge from 2027/28: £1.1m in that year, £1.1m in 2028/29, and £3.2m in 2029/30. The cumulative effect is £5.4m by the end of the MTFS period. The 2029/30 deficit is partly driven by £2.88m of contractual non-service inflation for which no mitigation is identified in this appendix.
findings.matters: A £5.4m accumulated deficit over four years means the council must make substantial service cuts, significantly raise council tax, or draw reserves down significantly. This indicates unresolved budget pressure and potential financial stress in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Investment income declining as proportion of budget while council increases borrowing to fund investments
findings.detail: The percentage of gross expenditure funded by investment income is forecast to drop from 5.9% in 2025/26 to 4.5% in 2026/27. Simultaneously, the amount of investments funded by borrowing is rising from £55.9m to £63.2m. Treasury management returns are also declining, forecast at 3.75% for 2026/27 versus 4.5% in 2025/26. This combination—rising leverage, falling yields, and declining proportional income—reduces the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: The council is increasing its debt-funded investment exposure at a time when those investments are returning less to support the General Fund budget, suggesting tightening finances and increased risk if market conditions deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Investment income proportion: 5.9% (2025/26) to 4.5% (2026/27); borrowing-funded investments: £55.9m (2025) to £63.2m (2027 forecast); treasury rate of return: 4.5% to 3.75%

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio shows £5.2m in losses with further write-downs anticipated
findings.detail: The council's investment property holdings are valued at £27.1m against a purchase cost of £32.3m, representing £5.2m in unrealized losses. Connect 38 Offices accounts for £1.5m of this loss (valued at £16.4m against £17.9m cost). A separate parcel of land has been written down entirely (£2.9m loss). The council flags that if 2025/26 audit valuations reveal further impairments, a revised investment strategy will be presented to Full Council addressing 'the impact of the loss on the security of investments and any revenue consequences'.
findings.matters: Asset values below purchase cost signal deteriorating commercial property market conditions and reduce the security underpinning the investment portfolio. The flagged expectation of further write-downs in the audit process suggests management anticipates additional losses.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 8 - Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development will not contribute revenue to the council for at least five years
findings.detail: The council has loaned £24.0m and invested £1.8m equity in Otterpool Park LLP, a Garden Town scheme. The document explicitly states that no capital receipts or contributions are anticipated during the entire Medium Term Financial Strategy period to 2030/31. The council's future capital investment plans do not require repayment of the equity; instead, long-term modelling assumes the authority will recover its total investment from the scheme's projected net proceeds. This is a 30-year development with no near-term financial return.
findings.matters: A major investment (£25.8m total exposure) with no anticipated contribution to council finances for five or more years ties up capital and reduces flexibility during budget pressures. The council is borrowing to fund this investment, increasing leverage while returns remain distant and uncertain.
findings.figures: £24.0m loaned, £1.8m equity invested; £11.3m loss allowance on the loan (net book value £12.7m); 30-year development period
findings.quote: No capital receipts or contributions from the development have been anticipated for the period of the latest Medium Term Financial Strategy to 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Balance sheet resources are forecast to decline by £17.7m through 2028/29 as the council draws down reserves to fund capital expenditure through internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council is using an 'internal borrowing' strategy, where it deploys cash balances and reserves to fund capital spending rather than raising external debt. However, available balance sheet resources are declining from £67.7m (2024/25) to £50.0m (2028/29). The document notes this drawdown will continue as the council uses reserves to meet approved capital expenditure plans and substitutes them for external borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and cushion against unexpected expenditure, and signal that the council will eventually need to rely more heavily on external borrowing
findings.figures: Balance sheet resources £67.7m (2024/25) to £57.2m (2026/27) to £50.0m (2028/29); internal borrowing increasing from £49.3m to £69.4m
findings.quote: The average balance is expected to reduce in the coming year as the council uses more of its reserves to meet its approved capital expenditure plans and also continues to use some of its cash balances in lieu of external borrowing (i.e internal borrowing).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Otterpool Park development lacks a confirmed strategic partner, and the council is excluding anticipated capital contributions from its financial forecasts pending partnership negotiations
findings.detail: Otterpool Park is identified as a major capital project requiring future funding through borrowing, but the council's financial planning explicitly excludes any future capital contributions or receipts from the scheme. The council is currently exploring partnership arrangements to fund the project. This creates uncertainty around whether the full borrowing burden will fall on the council or whether a partner will share the financing.
findings.matters: A major capital development without confirmed external financing or partnership creates financial uncertainty and means the council is forecasting higher debt levels than may ultimately be needed
findings.figures: Otterpool Park capital contributions explicitly excluded from liability benchmark and five-year projections
findings.quote: The liability benchmark currently excludes any future capital contributions or receipts from the Otterpool Park development to be used to reduce the CFR while the council explores finding a strategic partner to work with it on the project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: The council will borrow up to £122.9m in 2026/27 including replacing maturing debt, with further £17.5m borrowing required between 2025/26 and 2028/29 for capital investment
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow significantly from £156.8m (2024/25) to £192.3m (2026/27). This growth is driven by planned capital spending on major projects: Otterpool Park, FOLCA phase 2 town centre regeneration, and Hythe Pool refurbishment. The council is already holding £106.8m of borrowing as at 31 December 2025.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scope and sustainability of the council's capital programme and whether these major projects will generate sufficient returns or savings to service the debt
findings.figures: CFR growing from £156.8m (2024/25) to £192.3m (2026/27); borrowing forecast of £122.9m in 2026/27; additional borrowing £17.5m between 2025/26 and 2028/29
findings.quote: The Authority has an increasing CFR arising from its planned capital investment and will therefore be required to borrow up to a further £17.5m between 2025/26 and 2028/29, including replacing existing maturing debt.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery remains a challenge with 20% underspend in 2024/25, partly driven by slippage on the Otterpool project.
findings.detail: The capital programme delivered £13.576m against a budget of £17.050m (20% underspend). A significant portion relates to the 'Folkestone – A Brighter Future' project. The auditor recommends the council monitor delivery more closely and take corrective action. The Otterpool project is ongoing, and members are encouraged to review its progress closely.
findings.matters: Persistent capital slippage of 20% suggests either over-optimistic budgeting, delivery challenges, or both. For a lender, this signals whether infrastructure plans will be delivered as forecast, which affects both the council's operational capacity and its ability to deliver planned savings or revenue generation.
findings.figures: £13.576m outturn against £17.050m budget (20% underspend); significant portion relates to Folkestone – A Brighter Future project
findings.quote: In 2024/25, capital spend was approximately 20% under budget, a significant portion of which relates to the 'Folkestone – A Brighter Future' project. The Council should monitor delivery more closely to identify potential slippage and take corrective action.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Procurement practices show systemic weaknesses: waivers are routine, contract registers are incomplete, and contracts routinely expire before replacements are signed.
findings.detail: The council's procurement process relies on waivers driven by late engagement and minimal justification, exposing it to contractual risk. Contract management suffers from an incomplete register, inconsistent compliance, and no centralised supplier performance monitoring. Waivers were frequently required because contracts expired before new agreements were signed, forcing backdated agreements and reliance on supplier goodwill. These weaknesses have persisted for years and create non-compliance, financial exposure, and reputational risk.
findings.matters: Weak procurement controls mean the council may overpay for services, expose itself to legal challenge, or be unable to demonstrate value for money. The pattern of expiring contracts and backdated waivers suggests a structural capacity or process failure rather than isolated incidents.
findings.figures: No quantified impact disclosed
findings.quote: Waivers are often driven by late engagement from budget managers and minimal justification, exposing the Council to contractual risk. Contract management suffers from an incomplete register, inconsistent compliance, and lack of systematic performance monitoring, compounded by limitations in the current finance system. Some of these weaknesses have been in place for a number of years and need to be urgently addressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: The shared waste contract with Dover lacks sufficient governance controls to ensure service standards are met.
findings.detail: Folkestone & Hythe has limited authority over the waste management contract, which is managed entirely by Dover. Internal audit identified multiple weaknesses: Veolia self-assesses performance without independent verification and has failed to detect defects; penalty clauses are applied inconsistently; inspections are restricted to weekdays despite weekend service needs. These issues create financial inefficiencies and limit the council's ability to enforce standards.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's major contracts are adequately overseen and whether service failures could result in unbudgeted costs or reputational damage. Shared service arrangements with limited local control are a structural governance risk.
findings.figures: No specific figures on cost impact disclosed
findings.quote: The contract is managed by Dover on behalf of both councils, leaving Folkestone & Hythe reliant on Dover for decisions and oversight. Internal audit identified weaknesses, including Veolia self-assessing performance without detecting defects, ineffective application of penalty clauses, and limited inspections restricted to weekdays despite weekend service needs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: Princes Parade project formally closed with £3.4m write-off after unable to meet planning consent requirements
findings.detail: The council is formally closing the Princes Parade scheme and writing off approximately £3.4m in sunk costs in the 2025/26 financial statements. The auditor notes the decision to write off costs was supported by sound rationale, but remarks that value for money was not achieved. The write-off will be covered by the Financial Stability Reserve. The auditor has raised an improvement recommendation for a lessons learned exercise on project governance.
findings.matters: A £3.4m loss on a capital scheme signals weak project governance or planning assumptions. The scheme ran without formal documentation of the decision, and there is no prior lessons-learned process to prevent similar failures on major capital projects.
findings.figures: £3.4 million write-off; approximately 20% capital programme underspend (£3.474m under budget on £17.050m) in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Princes Parade project has been formally closed after the Council determined it could not meet planning consent requirements, resulting in a £3.4 million write-off. We note the final decision to write off sunk costs for the abandoned Princes Parade project was supported by a sound rationale, however it is unfortunate that value for money for this investment was not achieved, and a review needs to take place so that lessons should be learned for future programmes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 6. Folkestone and Hythe District Council Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Final
findings.headline: A projected funding gap of £3.6m by April 2028 remains unresolved heading into Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The council has identified a cumulative deficit of £3.6m by 1 April 2028. This issue has now been raised three years running (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25). The auditor notes the council holds £18m in reserves as of 31 March 2025 and has not yet escalated this to a significant weakness, but warns this could change if appropriate steps are not taken to achieve a sustainable financial position before LGR and to transfer appropriate reserves to the successor council.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council will hand over a sustainable position to its successor authority in three years, or whether financial pressures will persist. Three consecutive years of the same warning suggests neither savings plans nor structural changes have yet closed the gap.

findings.quote: A medium-term funding gap has been identified, with a projected cumulative deficit of £3.6m by 1 April 2028. The Council must take steps to strengthen its financial position and ensure an appropriate level of reserves is available for transfer to the successor authority ahead of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).

news_drafts.headline: Folkestone and Hythe's underlying need to borrow rose £15.8m to £172.6m in 2025/26, driven by housing and Otterpool Park
news_drafts.lead:
Folkestone and Hythe District Council's capital financing requirement (CFR), the total it has spent on long-lasting assets that it has not yet paid for, rose by £15.8m in 2025/26 to £172.6m, from £156.8m a year earlier. The figure is in the treasury management annual report going to the council's Cabinet on 14 October 2026.

The report attributes the rise to capital spending, meaning money spent on things that last, during the year. That included £9.3m on projects in the housing revenue account (the separate, rent-funded account for the council's own homes) and £4.1m on the Otterpool Park Garden Town development. A further £0.8m went on Changing Tides and £0.1m on a waste vehicle.

The council paid for the increase in two ways. It took £10.3m of new external borrowing, which brought its external loans to £117.8m. It also raised its internal borrowing by £5.5m to £54.8m. Internal borrowing means using the council's own cash balances to pay for capital spending instead of taking out a loan. That saves interest but uses up cash the council would otherwise hold. The £54.8m covers 32% of the CFR.

The report describes this as the council's strategy to reduce risk and keep interest costs low, by holding borrowing and investments below their underlying levels.

news_drafts.headline: Folkestone and Hythe projects £504k deficit despite break-even budget as reserves draw down 13.5%
news_drafts.lead: Folkestone and Hythe council is projecting a revenue deficit of £504k for 2026/27, a £503k adverse variance from its budgeted break-even position, according to Q1 budget monitoring reported to its Finance and Performance Scrutiny Sub-Committee on 29 September. The shortfall emerges despite the council drawing down £3.079m (13.5%) of its reserves to cover service pressures and capital projects. Housing benefits are overspending by £456k, adding to broader service variances totalling £1.438m above budget. The council is responding by increasing its General Fund capital borrowing by £3.4m to £14.554m, and funding an additional £935k of capital expenditure from reserves rather than external finance. Reserves are projected to fall from £22.7m to £19.4m by year-end.
